Commenter was surprised Gaudi 3 uses HBM2e, the memory Nvidia's A100 used in 2020. With 8 stacks, though, it reaches about 3.7TB/s, comparable to the H100's 3.4TB/s on 5 stacks of HBM3. They noted the older HBM may be easier to get, since HBM3 is in short supply.

Complaint that the speedup numbers are misleading: Intel compares H100/H200 throughput at lower batch sizes against Gaudi 3 at higher batch sizes, and throughput rises heavily with batch size. That makes it hard to tell which inference scenarios Gaudi 3 actually wins.
Gaudi 3 has PCIe 4.0 versus PCIe 5.0 on the H100, which offers 2x the bandwidth. Probably not a deal-breaker, but it's strange for Intel of all vendors to lag behind in PCIe.

Skeptic asks whether Intel will keep this product line alive for more than a few years. They say they were bitten before by building products on Intel's non-x86 offerings, which Intel killed off and then failed to support. They still hope it succeeds so there are alternative accelerators.

Praise for Gaudi 3 using the open OAM (Open Accelerator Module) interface instead of a proprietary connector like Nvidia's SXM. Because the interface is open, these devices may still have a life for hobbyists in 8–10 years instead of going straight to the bin.
Vector floating-point performance is only 14 TFLOPS FP32 and 28 TFLOPS FP16, so Gaudi 3 is weak for workloads that don't fit the matrix processing units.

Complaint that Intel gives no useful matrix-multiply detail: which MMA type and dimension combinations Gaudi supports, and how many ops per second in practice. '64,000 in parallel' does not tell much. Another user asked for a Gaudi equivalent of Nvidia's PTX ISA reference.

On the 24 integrated 200Gb Ethernet ports: a single 200Gbit fiber cable probably costs thousands of dollars. That makes cabling each card very expensive, never mind the switches. 'Simultaneously impressive and disappointing.'

Using Ethernet for Gaudi 3's interconnect could be a win if it matches NVLink performance, because everybody knows how to manage Ethernet and few know how to manage an NVLink network. But the 'in the wild' showing was a very controlled environment, the lower-power cards still draw about 600W, and no pricing was given.

A GPU cloud operator says Gaudi 3's 24x200G ports are already outdated, since they currently run 400G per GPU and 800G at the spine. They also dislike the switching fabric being on the card, because a fabric failure loses the whole card. They prefer composable PCIe fabrics.
User asked where Gaudi 3 instances can actually be used and at what hourly price, pointing to a lack of clear rental availability.

An infra/HPC developer disputes Intel's 'fully programmable Tensor Processor Cores' claim. They have yet to see anyone write custom kernels for Intel Gaudi, and say tensor cores on any platform are limited to dense tiled matmul with few numeric types.

On Gaudi 3 costing half as much as the H100: Nvidia's H100 margins are reportedly huge, so Nvidia can afford to cut prices. Nvidia's software toolchain advantage is also significant, which tempers the price edge, though the commenter welcomes the competition.
